candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: The simultaneous claims that God is all-loving, God is all-powerful, and suffering exists create the traditional philosophical problem of suffering.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduced Ehrman before the uninterrupted opening statement containing this argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This logical triad directly frames the central tension between divine love and power and the acknowledged existence of worldly suffering.
candidates.contextSummary: After describing his experience teaching biblical approaches to suffering, Ehrman formalizes the core philosophical conflict that structures his skeptical case.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: The Bible's prevalent prophetic explanation that suffering is divine punishment for sin is difficult to reconcile with innocent suffering.
candidates.attributionBasis: The argument occurs within Ehrman's continuous opening statement after his survey of biblical responses begins.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move challenges a prominent scriptural theodicy by contrasting punishment for wrongdoing with concrete cases in which sufferers are innocent.
candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman identifies punishment for sin as a recurring prophetic account, explains its logic, and then argues that undeserved affliction undermines it.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: Biblical apocalyptic writers attribute suffering to the devil and hostile cosmic forces rather than to God's punitive action.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker remains Ehrman throughout this uninterrupted comparison of distinct biblical explanations of suffering.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This alternative is load-bearing because it demonstrates that scripture contains materially different causal accounts of suffering rather than one unified answer.
candidates.contextSummary: Continuing his biblical survey, Ehrman contrasts the prophetic punishment model with an apocalyptic model centered on divine enemies causing worldly misery.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: One narrative in Job portrays extreme suffering as a divinely permitted test of whether a righteous person will remain faithful.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is part of Ehrman's uninterrupted opening statement and his sequential account of biblical explanations.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The Job narrative supplies another major theodicy while intensifying the moral problem through divinely permitted suffering imposed on an exceptionally righteous person.
candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman recounts the wager involving Job and explains that the resulting deaths and personal anguish function as a test rather than punishment.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: Most of Job offers no intelligible explanation for innocent suffering and instead denies the sufferer standing to question God.
candidates.attributionBasis: Ehrman explicitly distinguishes this portion of Job while continuing the same uninterrupted opening presentation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument challenges an appeal to divine mystery by portraying it as a refusal to explain pain and misery rather than a substantive reconciliation.
candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman contrasts Job's wager narrative with the book's other treatment, where divine magnificence and human insignificance displace the demand for justification.
